title: Mapping which TAIG open problems have public tooling vs. none

# Mapping which TAIG open problems have public tooling vs. none

**Problem:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance lists many problems across capacities (access, verification) and targets (data, compute, models), but it is unclear which actually have usable public tools/datasets and which are stuck at the proposal stage, a gap that misallocates beginner researcher effort.

**Direction:** Vary the open-problems taxonomy into a tooling-coverage survey experiment: for each listed problem, systematically search for public datasets/code/benchmarks addressing it, code maturity (none / proposal / prototype / deployed) with a fixed rubric, and produce a coverage map highlighting high-importance/low-tooling cells.

**Why it matters:** Produces a reusable 'where to contribute' map for technical AI governance, valuable to the whole community and especially newcomers. Pure literature/web survey, no lab access, no training.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (Reuel et al., arXiv:2407.14981; taig.stanford.edu); Interface-EU publication.

# Do safety-framework commitments name independent third parties, or only internal review?

**Problem:** Third-party verification of safety claims is a flagship open problem, but the extent to which lab frameworks actually delegate evaluation/decision authority to external bodies (vs. self-assessment) has not been measured across labs.

**Direction:** Vary commitment coding to focus on the actor axis: extract every governance/verification commitment from public frameworks and code who holds authority (internal team / board / external auditor / government / none specified), then quantify the share of safety-critical decisions that remain fully internal per lab.

**Why it matters:** Directly measures the credibility of self-governance, central to the third-party-verification open problem, and gives auditors a concrete 'internal-only decision' count. Public text, beginner rubric coding.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (third-party verification/auditing); METR Common Elements; Evaluating AI Companies' Frontier Safety Frameworks (arXiv:2512.01166).

title: Replicating the 'no explicit AGI control plan' finding across a wider company set

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the 'no explicit AGI control plan' finding across a wider company set

**Problem:** FLI evaluated 7 labs and found none with explicit superintelligence control plans, but smaller frontier-adjacent companies (e.g., Mistral, Cohere, regional labs) were excluded, leaving the breadth of the planning gap unknown.

**Direction:** Vary the population from FLI's 7 labs to a broader set of ~15 AI companies: apply a minimal control-plan rubric (acknowledges risk? names an approach? commits to a stop/escalation condition? assigns responsibility?) to each company's public statements, and report how the planning gap scales beyond the frontier seven.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether the existential-planning vacuum is a frontier-seven phenomenon or industry-wide, informing how broadly governance must reach. Public statements only, beginner-feasible.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Summer/Winter 2025 (7 labs, existential safety gap); MIRI 'AI Governance to Avoid Extinction' (2025).

title: Do the FLI AI Safety Index grades track public commitments or actual disclosures?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses reliability of a widely-cited safety index, a recognized governance auditing problem.

original_idea.body:
# Do the FLI AI Safety Index grades track public commitments or actual disclosures?

**Problem:** FLI's AI Safety Index gives labs grades (none above C+ in Winter 2025) across 33 indicators, but it is unclear whether grade movements over time reflect new safety behavior or merely more polished public communication.

**Direction:** Treat the FLI Index as a fixed experimental instrument and run a follow-up: scrape the public-facing safety documents (RSPs, system cards, blog posts) FLI cites for each lab across the 2024 and 2025 editions, and use simple NLP (commitment-counting, hedging-word detection, verifiability tagging) to test whether grade changes correlate more with volume/tone of disclosure than with concrete, verifiable commitments. Report correlation between text features and grade deltas.

**Why it matters:** If index grades are driven by communication style rather than substance, third parties relying on them for procurement or policy could be misled. Building a transparent, reproducible re-scoring harness is exactly the kind of audit infrastructure valuable outside any lab.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index 2024/Winter 2025 (33 indicators, GPA grading); CLAIM.md note that estimated/unverified safety claims are unreliable; Open Problem: third-party-auditable verification methods.

title: Replicating the FLI 'existential safety' D-grade finding with an LLM panel
quick_reasoning: Addresses scalable automated safety auditing of existential-safety grades, a clear governance topic.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the FLI 'existential safety' D-grade finding with an LLM panel

**Problem:** Every lab scored D or below on 'existential safety' in the FLI Index, judged by a 7-expert human panel. Whether that judgment is reproducible by cheaper automated raters (relevant for scaling audits) is untested.

**Direction:** Follow up the FLI panel result by building an LLM-as-judge re-scoring of the same publicly cited evidence against FLI's published rubric, then compare LLM scores to the human panel scores. Measure inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa), sensitivity to prompt phrasing, and whether the LLM reproduces the existential-safety failure pattern.

**Why it matters:** If automated raters can cheaply reproduce expert safety grades, low-resource civil-society groups could run continuous audits. If they cannot, that itself is an important negative result about automated governance evaluation.

**Relevant context:** FLI Index expert-panel methodology; CLAUDE.md rubric requirement for numeric scores; Open Problem on international consensus on evaluation methodologies.

title: Is MIRI's governance pivot mirrored across technical AI safety orgs?

# Is MIRI's governance pivot mirrored across technical AI safety orgs?

**Problem:** MIRI's 2025 pivot from alignment to governance was flagged as surprising and as possibly signaling a broader belief that technical alignment alone is insufficient, but no systematic check exists on whether other technical orgs are shifting too.

**Direction:** Follow up by assembling a corpus of public outputs (blog posts, papers, job listings, agendas) from ~15 technical AI safety orgs over 2021-2026 and using simple keyword/topic classification plus publication-date trends to quantify the share of governance- vs alignment-focused output over time. Test whether MIRI's pivot is an outlier or part of a field-wide trend.

**Why it matters:** Understanding whether the technical safety community is collectively de-prioritizing pure alignment shapes where new researchers should invest. The analysis needs only public text and is squarely outside-lab work.

**Relevant context:** Recent Surprising Results: MIRI 2025 governance agenda pivot; Generation Strategy Hint FR68 (MIRI strategic pivot needs follow-up).

title: Re-running the safetywashing capability-correlation test on 2025-era governance benchmarks

original_idea.body:
# Re-running the safetywashing capability-correlation test on 2025-era governance benchmarks

**Problem:** Ren et al. (2024) showed many safety benchmarks correlate strongly with raw capabilities ('safetywashing'). Newer governance-relevant evals (refusal, jailbreak-robustness, agentic-misuse benchmarks released in 2025) were not in that study.

**Direction:** Follow up by applying the published safetywashing methodology (their open GitHub code computes capability-correlation) to a fresh set of 2025 safety/governance benchmarks using public leaderboard scores across open models. Report which new benchmarks are capability-entangled and which measure something orthogonal, extending their analysis.

**Why it matters:** Regulators increasingly cite benchmark scores as evidence of safety; knowing which 2025 benchmarks are confounded by capability prevents policy from rewarding mere scaling. Uses public scores and existing open-source code, no training.

**Relevant context:** Ren et al. 2024 'Safetywashing' (NeurIPS, open code at centerforaisafety/safetywashing); Generation Strategy Hint FR67 (vary AI Safety Index / benchmark methodology).

title: Does inference scaling actually let sub-threshold models match above-threshold ones?
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific compute-threshold governance loophole with a clear empirical test of a live safety-policy assumption.

original_idea.body:
# Does inference scaling actually let sub-threshold models match above-threshold ones?

**Problem:** A 2025 analysis argued compute-threshold governance (10^25/10^26 FLOP) is undermined because inference scaling could amplify a sub-threshold model to above-threshold capability, but the claim is largely theoretical.

**Direction:** Follow up with a small empirical test: take a small open model below any plausible threshold and measure how much its scores on dangerous-capability-proxy benchmarks (e.g., reasoning, tool-use) improve under increased inference compute (best-of-n, chain-of-thought, self-consistency) on a single consumer GPU. Quantify the effective 'capability gain' from inference and compare to the training-compute gaps the policy assumes.

**Why it matters:** If a few hours of inference scaling closes a large fraction of the gap, FLOP-threshold-based laws (EU AI Act, EO 14110) need rethinking. Cheap, training-free, and directly tests a live governance assumption.

**Relevant context:** 'Inference Scaling Reshapes AI Governance' (arXiv 2503.05705); compute thresholds 10^25 (EU) / 10^26 (US); Open Problem: compute governance mechanisms.

title: Auditing the LLM-based AI Incident Database classification pipeline for systematic bias

# Auditing the LLM-based AI Incident Database classification pipeline for systematic bias

**Problem:** Recent work uses LLM pipelines guided by the OECD framework to classify AIID incidents by risk taxonomy and severity, but the reliability and bias of these automated classifications has not been independently checked.

**Direction:** Follow up the LLM-classification result by taking a sample of AIID incidents, having an LLM classify them under the MIT AI Risk Taxonomy / CSET harm severity scale, and testing: (a) agreement between models/prompts, (b) whether incident attributes (domain, named company, language) predict severity assignments, surfacing systematic bias. Hand-label a small gold set to estimate accuracy.

**Why it matters:** If automated incident classification is biased (e.g., under-rating certain harm types), governance dashboards built on it mislead policymakers. Incident-response infrastructure is an explicit open problem and this is pure public-data analysis.

**Relevant context:** LLM-Based Analysis of the AI Incident Database (IEEE 2025); AIID >1,300 incidents; Open Problem: national AI incident response frameworks (NTSB analogy).

title: Does the gap between FLI top-3 and the rest reflect resources or willingness?

# Does the gap between FLI top-3 and the rest reflect resources or willingness?

**Problem:** FLI found a persistent divide between top performers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind) and the rest (xAI, Meta), with biggest gaps in risk assessment and information sharing. Whether this divide is explained by company resources or by stated philosophy is untested.

**Direction:** Follow up by collecting public proxies (org size, safety-team headcount from job postings, training-compute estimates from Epoch, public stance statements) for each graded company and regressing FLI domain scores against them. Test which factor best predicts the safety-framework / information-sharing gap.

**Why it matters:** If the gap is willingness rather than capacity, policy should mandate disclosure rather than subsidize safety teams; if it is capacity, the opposite. Uses only public data and the existing FLI scores.

**Relevant context:** FLI Index domain breakdown (risk assessment, safety framework, info sharing gaps); Epoch AI compute tracking data (Key Datasets).

title: Do frontier safety frameworks actually specify falsifiable capability thresholds?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets falsifiability/enforceability of capability thresholds, a specific AI Safety governance problem.

original_idea.body:
# Do frontier safety frameworks actually specify falsifiable capability thresholds?

**Problem:** Twelve frontier developers published safety frameworks after the Seoul Summit, but assessments note capability-threshold setting is 'nascent' and experts disagree on adequacy. How concrete vs vague the thresholds actually are has not been systematically measured.

**Direction:** Follow up the framework-evaluation literature with a structured content analysis: code each published framework's capability thresholds on a rubric (quantitative vs qualitative, measurable trigger vs vague, named eval vs none, committed pause vs aspirational). Score and rank frameworks on threshold concreteness, extending prior grading-rubric work to the specific axis of falsifiability.

**Why it matters:** Vague thresholds make frameworks unenforceable; a public concreteness scorecard pressures labs and informs regulators using these frameworks as reference points. Pure document analysis, replicable outside any lab.

**Relevant context:** METR Frontier Safety Policies; 'Evaluating AI Providers' Frontier Safety Frameworks' (arXiv 2512.01166, 65 weighted criteria); 'A Grading Rubric for AI Safety Frameworks' (arXiv 2409.08751).

title: Measuring drift between successive RSP versions: are commitments strengthening or eroding?

# Measuring drift between successive RSP versions: are commitments strengthening or eroding?

**Problem:** Labs revise their Responsible Scaling Policies / safety frameworks over time, and observers worry commitments quietly weaken, but no quantitative tracking of version-to-version changes exists.

**Direction:** Follow up by collecting archived versions of 3-4 labs' frontier safety frameworks (Wayback Machine / git histories), diffing them, and classifying each substantive change as strengthening, weakening, or neutral against a published rubric. Produce a longitudinal 'commitment drift' timeline.

**Why it matters:** If voluntary commitments erode silently, that is strong evidence that the EU AI Act gap between voluntary codes and enforceable standards matters. A reproducible diff-tracker is durable governance infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** METR FSP tracker; EU AI Act Open Problem (voluntary vs enforceable gap); Anthropic RSP / OpenAI Preparedness / GDM Frontier Safety Framework versions.

# How verifiable are EU GPAI Code of Practice safety commitments by an outside party?

**Problem:** The EU GPAI Code has 12 commitments (10 in Safety & Security) that signatories rely on for simplified compliance, but it is unclear how many can be checked by anyone outside the company.

**Direction:** Follow up the Code's publication by coding each of the 12 commitments on a verifiability scale (externally verifiable from public artifacts / verifiable only with internal access / self-attestation only). Then test against early signatories' published documentation whether the externally verifiable commitments are actually evidenced. Produce a verifiability scorecard.

**Why it matters:** Enforcement begins August 2026 focused on checking Code commitments; if most are self-attestation, third-party oversight is impossible and the regime is weak. Directly addresses the auditable-verification open problem with public-only analysis.

**Relevant context:** EU GPAI Code of Practice (12 commitments, Articles 53/55); enforcement starts 2026-08-02; Open Problem: third-party-auditable verification.

# Does California SB 53 transparency-report structure match what labs already disclose?

**Problem:** California's SB 53 (effective 2026) mandates specific transparency-report fields (release date, intended uses, catastrophic-risk-assessment summaries, third-party involvement). Whether existing system cards already cover these fields or leave large gaps is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Follow up the law's passage with a gap analysis: build a checklist from SB 53's required fields and score recent frontier system cards (Claude, GPT, Gemini) for coverage. Quantify compliance distance and which mandated fields are most commonly missing before the law takes effect.

**Why it matters:** A pre-enforcement baseline shows how much real change SB 53 will force vs ratify existing practice, informing whether the first US frontier law has teeth. Public documents only, replicable annually.

**Relevant context:** California SB 53 TFAIA (signed 2025-09, effective 2026-01); 'Blueprints of Trust' system-card framework (arXiv 2509.20394); Open Problem: operationalizing safety into deployment practices.

quick_reasoning: Directly addresses open-weight release governance risks via a scoped index adaptation.

# Extending the AI Safety Index methodology to open-weight model releasers

**Problem:** The FLI Index covers six closed-model companies, but the surprising-results note suggests applying its methodology to additional dimensions. Open-weight releasers (Meta, Mistral, open-source orgs) pose distinct governance risks not captured by the current index.

**Direction:** Follow up by adapting FLI's indicator rubric to open-weight-specific risks (irreversibility of release, downstream fine-tuning safeguards, removed-safety-filter monitoring) and scoring a set of open-weight releasers against the adapted rubric using their public release docs and licenses. Report scores and methodology adaptations.

**Why it matters:** Open-weight release is a medium/long-horizon, hard-to-reverse threat that frontier labs and the existing index under-cover; an open-weight safety index is valuable governance infrastructure with no lab dependency.

**Relevant context:** Generation Strategy Hint FR67 (apply AI Safety Index methodology to additional dimensions); FLI Index 33-indicator rubric; Open Problem: operationalizing safety objectives into deployment practices.

title: Do export-controlled FLOP thresholds line up with where dangerous capabilities actually emerge?

# Do export-controlled FLOP thresholds line up with where dangerous capabilities actually emerge?

**Problem:** Compute-threshold governance assumes capability (and risk) scales predictably with training FLOP, but the threshold values (10^25/10^26) were set with limited public evidence on where dangerous-capability inflection points occur.

**Direction:** Follow up the threshold-policy debate with an empirical mapping: using Epoch's public training-compute estimates and public benchmark scores across many models, plot safety-relevant capability proxies (deception, persuasion, cyber, bio-knowledge benchmarks) against training compute and test whether thresholds sit near any inflection / discontinuity. Report whether current thresholds are well-placed.

**Why it matters:** If risk does not jump at the legislated thresholds, the policy either over- or under-regulates. This is a direct empirical follow-up usable by regulators, built entirely on public datasets.

**Relevant context:** Compute thresholds 10^25 (EU AI Act) / 10^26 (US EO 14110); Epoch AI compute tracking (Key Datasets); 'The Role of Compute Thresholds for AI Governance' (law-ai.org).

title: Is the FLI Index's information-sharing weakness visible in actual whistleblower/incident disclosure behavior?

# Is the FLI Index's information-sharing weakness visible in actual whistleblower/incident disclosure behavior?

**Problem:** FLI flagged 'information sharing' as a top weakness across labs, but the index measures stated policies, not observed disclosure behavior such as voluntary incident reporting.

**Direction:** Follow up by cross-referencing each graded lab against the AI Incident Database and public incident reports: count voluntarily self-reported vs externally-discovered incidents per lab, and test whether labs with low FLI information-sharing scores also self-report less. Triangulate stated policy against revealed behavior.

**Why it matters:** Reveals whether information-sharing grades predict real transparency, validating (or invalidating) the index as a behavioral proxy and informing mandatory-incident-reporting design. Uses two public datasets, no lab access.

**Relevant context:** FLI Index information-sharing domain; AIID (>1,300 incidents); Open Problem: national incident-response frameworks; The Future Society on incident playbooks.

# Reproducing dangerous-capability eval results from labs' own published system cards

**Problem:** FLI found only three of seven labs demonstrate meaningful dangerous-capability testing, and labs report these results in system cards; but third parties rarely check whether the reported eval numbers are reproducible on open analogues.

**Direction:** Follow up by selecting a few dangerous-capability evals labs report in system cards that have open implementations (e.g., a published jailbreak or cyber-knowledge benchmark), running them on accessible open models on a single GPU, and comparing the shape/trend of results to what labs report. Document where independent reproduction is feasible vs blocked by missing methodology.

**Why it matters:** Reproducibility is the foundation of third-party audit; documenting which reported safety evals can even be independently checked maps the verification frontier. Training-free, public-eval-based.

**Relevant context:** FLI finding on dangerous-capability testing; Open Problem: third-party-auditable verification; 'Safety Under Scaffolding' (arXiv 2603.10044) on eval-condition sensitivity.

# Does eval scaffolding sensitivity threaten governance reliance on safety scores?

**Problem:** Recent work ('Safety Under Scaffolding') suggests measured safety depends heavily on evaluation conditions, but the governance implication (that policy-cited scores are fragile) has not been quantified on the specific benchmarks regulators cite.

**Direction:** Follow up by taking one or two safety benchmarks referenced in governance documents, running an open model under several reasonable scaffolding variations (system-prompt phrasing, tool access, sampling temperature, few-shot) on a single GPU, and measuring how much the safety score swings. Report the variance and what it implies for citing a single number in policy.

**Why it matters:** If a safety score swings widely with harmless scaffolding choices, mandating disclosure of a single number is meaningless without standardized protocols, an explicit international-consensus open problem.

**Relevant context:** 'Safety Under Scaffolding' (arXiv 2603.10044); Open Problem: international consensus on evaluation methodologies; CLAUDE.md rubric/reliability emphasis.

**Problem:** Audit findings report that when a prompt filter, toxicity monitor, and access controls live in different vendors, no single record captures the full governance picture, and auditors find gaps 'at the seams', but this has not been systematically demonstrated.

Produce a taxonomy of seam-gaps and a minimal unified-log prototype.

**Why it matters:** Builds a small piece of monitoring/audit infrastructure for the increasingly common composed-AI-system case, directly addressing the agentic-traceability gap auditors flag, with no proprietary dependencies.

**Relevant context:** 2025 audit findings on fragmented governance / seam-gaps; 'Incident Analysis for AI Agents' (arXiv 2508.14231); Open Problem: operationalizing safety into deployment practices.

**Problem:** The AIID is limited to publicly reported incidents, and recent work on agentic-AI incident analysis suggests agent failures lack traceability, hinting these incidents may be systematically under-represented in the database.

**Direction:** Follow up by classifying recent AIID incidents (2024-2026) on whether they involve agentic/autonomous behavior using a coded rubric, then comparing the agentic share over time against the known rapid rise of agentic deployments. Test for an under-counting gap and characterize what agentic incidents do get reported.

**Why it matters:** If agentic incidents are invisible to the main public database, incident-response frameworks will be built blind to the fastest-growing risk class, a medium-horizon threat labs deprioritize. Public-data only.

title: Do the 65-criteria framework assessments agree with the FLI Index on lab ordering?

Investigate the disagreements to surface which methodological choices (weighting, indicator selection) drive divergent governance verdicts.

**Why it matters:** If two reputable indices disagree on who is safest, single-index policy reliance is risky and the field needs methodology convergence, the international-consensus open problem. Combines two public scoring datasets, no lab access.

**Relevant context:** FLI Index (33 indicators); 'Evaluating AI Providers' Frontier Safety Frameworks' (arXiv 2512.01166, 65 criteria); Generation Strategy Hint FR67; Open Problem on evaluation-methodology consensus.

original_idea.body:
# Does the MACHIAVELLI anti-correlation generalize to newer agentic-safety benchmarks?

**Problem:** Ren et al. found most safety benchmarks correlate with capabilities, but MACHIAVELLI uniquely showed negative correlation, suggesting it measures a distinct property. Whether newer agentic / power-seeking benchmarks share this rare orthogonality is unknown.

**Direction:** Follow up by computing capability-correlations (using the published safetywashing method) for a set of recent agentic-behavior / deception benchmarks across open models with public scores, and testing which (if any) replicate MACHIAVELLI's anti-correlation pattern, flagging genuinely capability-independent safety signals.

**Why it matters:** Identifying benchmarks that measure safety independent of scale is exactly what Ren et al. called for and what regulators need to avoid rewarding capability as safety. Public scores + existing open code, no training.

**Relevant context:** Ren et al. 2024 'Safetywashing' (MACHIAVELLI anti-correlation; open code); Generation Strategy Hint FR67; CLAUDE.md rubric-for-scores rule.

title: Are 'catastrophic risk assessment' summaries in transparency reports informative or boilerplate?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses whether mandated catastrophic-risk disclosures are substantive, a transparency-governance concern.

original_idea.body:
# Are 'catastrophic risk assessment' summaries in transparency reports informative or boilerplate?

**Problem:** SB 53 and the EU Code both require summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments, and the surprising worry is that mandated summaries collapse into uninformative boilerplate that satisfies the letter but not the spirit of disclosure.

**Direction:** Follow up by collecting existing catastrophic-risk / safety-case sections from frontier system cards and frameworks and scoring them on an informativeness rubric (specific quantified claims, named threats, residual-risk acknowledgment vs vague reassurance). Use text-similarity to detect boilerplate reuse across companies and over versions.

**Why it matters:** If mandated risk summaries are boilerplate, the new US/EU transparency laws produce paperwork not insight, a critical finding for regulators designing disclosure standards. Public-document analysis only.

**Relevant context:** California SB 53 catastrophic-risk-summary requirement; EU GPAI Code Safety & Security chapter; Open Problem: operationalizing safety objectives; 'Blueprints of Trust' (arXiv 2509.20394).

title: Replicating the AI Safety Index Scoring Rubric on a Set of Open-Weight Model Developers
quick_reasoning: Directly extends a respected safety-governance benchmark to under-covered open-weight developers.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the AI Safety Index Scoring Rubric on a Set of Open-Weight Model Developers

**Problem:** The FLI AI Safety Index grades a small set of frontier labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, xAI, Meta, plus Chinese labs) across six governance domains using a 35-indicator expert-panel rubric. Smaller open-weight developers (Mistral, AI2/Allen Institute, EleutherAI, Cohere, Stability, Together) are not scored, leaving a transparency gap about the safety practices of the open-model ecosystem that many downstream deployers rely on.

**Direction:** Take the published AI Safety Index indicator rubric (governance, information sharing, risk assessment, safety frameworks) and apply it as a structured document-review exercise to 6-8 open-weight developers, scoring each indicator from public artifacts (model cards, safety policies, responsible-use docs, blog posts). Build a simple scoring spreadsheet, document evidence per indicator, and produce a comparative grade table plus a discussion of which indicators are systematically un-met by open developers and why.

**Why it matters:** Extends a respected governance benchmark to a deprioritized but high-leverage slice of the ecosystem (open models), revealing whether open developers' safety reporting lags frontier labs. This is exactly the kind of diffuse, no-lab-resources evaluation that is valuable outside major labs and informs deployment governance.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in FLI AI Safety Index (Summer/Winter 2025) which uses six domains and 35 indicators scored A+ to F. Methodology is public and replicable as document review. No model inference required; only public artifacts.

title: Replicating Model-Card Transparency Scoring on Hugging Face's Most-Downloaded Open Models
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses safety-critical transparency gaps in widely-deployed open models.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Model-Card Transparency Scoring on Hugging Face's Most-Downloaded Open Models

**Problem:** The AI Transparency Atlas evaluated 50 mostly-frontier models with a weighted 8-section/23-subsection rubric and found most providers below 60% compliance, with deception, hallucination, and child-safety disclosures the weakest. It did not focus on the long tail of widely-downloaded open models that power countless downstream apps.

**Direction:** Reimplement the Atlas weighted transparency rubric (safety evaluation 25%, critical risk 20%, etc.) as a manual + lightweight-LLM scoring pipeline, then apply it to the top 30-40 most-downloaded text-generation models on Hugging Face. Quantify which safety-critical sections are missing, compare open vs. provider-hosted cards, and report aggregate points lost per category.

**Why it matters:** Surfaces systematic transparency gaps in the models people actually deploy, providing governance-relevant evidence for documentation standards. Needs only public model cards and a single GPU (optional, for LLM-assisted scoring), making it ideal counterfactual work outside labs.

**Relevant context:** Based on AI Transparency Atlas (arXiv 2512.12443), which scored 50 models and 100 HF cards, finding 947 unique section names and large deficits in deception/hallucination/child-safety disclosures. Rubric and findings are public.

title: Replicating Multilingual Jailbreak Refusal-Rate Gaps on Open-Weight Models in Latin American Languages
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets multilingual jailbreak/refusal safety gaps with a well-scoped open-model experiment.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Multilingual Jailbreak Refusal-Rate Gaps on Open-Weight Models in Latin American Languages

**Problem:** Prior work shows low-resource languages are roughly 3x more likely to elicit harmful content than English, but the canonical studies focus on English, African languages (Afrikaans, Kiswahili, isiXhosa, isiZulu), and a few high-resource languages, and mostly on commercial models. The robustness of OPEN-weight models in Latin American indigenous and regional languages (e.g., Guarani, Quechua, Nahuatl, Rioplatense Spanish slang) is unstudied.

**Direction:** Replicate the multilingual jailbreak/refusal-rate methodology (translate a fixed set of harmful prompts, measure refusal vs. compliance) on 3-4 small open-weight instruct models, swapping in Latin American low-resource languages as the twist. Use a held-out benign control set to separate genuine refusal from translation failure, and report refusal-rate deltas by language and by harm category.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies a safety-equity governance gap directly relevant to a BAISH (Buenos Aires) audience and to multilingual deployment policy. Uses only public open models and translation, no lab infrastructure, and targets a diffuse fairness-of-safety problem labs underinvest in.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Multilingual Jailbreak Challenges' (ICLR24, ~3x harm in low-resource languages) and 'Multilingual jailbreaking of LLMs using low-resource languages' (arXiv 2605.18239) with African-language refusal-rate tables. Twist = Latin American languages + open models.

title: Replicating OpenAI's Model Spec Eval Harness on Open-Weight Models Without a Published Spec
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses behavioral-norm alignment (honesty, refusal, instruction hierarchy) of open models as a governance standard.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating OpenAI's Model Spec Eval Harness on Open-Weight Models Without a Published Spec

**Problem:** OpenAI's open-source Model Spec Evals (596 prompts, 225 focus areas, 1-7 compliance grading on Inspect) measure adherence to OpenAI's own spec and report rising compliance from GPT-4o (72%) to GPT-5 Thinking (89%). Open-weight models (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma) have no published spec and have never been scored against this rubric, so we don't know whether they implicitly satisfy widely-shared norms (honesty, refusal handling, instruction hierarchy).

**Direction:** Run the public Model Spec Eval harness against 3-4 open-weight instruct models on a single GPU, treating the OpenAI Model Spec as a de-facto cross-vendor norm. Report per-category compliance, identify where open models diverge most (e.g., instruction hierarchy, sensitive-topic handling), and discuss the governance implication of evaluating models against a spec they never adopted.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether shared behavioral norms transfer to open models, informing whether a common spec could serve as an interoperable governance standard. Uses fully open tooling and open models, no proprietary access.

**Relevant context:** Based on openai/model_spec_evals (GitHub) and 'Introducing Model Spec Evals' (596 prompts, Inspect AI, 1-7 grading). SpecEval (arXiv 2509.02464) provides a complementary auditing approach across 16 models.

title: Replicating SpecEval Spec-Adherence Auditing With a Single Open Grader Model to Test Judge Dependence
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses robustness of audit methods underpinning third-party safety verification.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating SpecEval Spec-Adherence Auditing With a Single Open Grader Model to Test Judge Dependence

**Problem:** SpecEval audits models against their providers' specs by parsing behavioral statements, generating prompts, and using a (typically strong, proprietary) judge model to score adherence across 16 models. A governance concern is judge dependence: if conclusions about a vendor's compliance flip when you swap the judge, the audit is not robust enough to support policy.

**Direction:** Replicate a small slice of the SpecEval pipeline (a few dozen behavioral statements from one public spec) but make the twist swapping the proprietary judge for a small OPEN judge model. Re-score the same target responses with both an open judge and a stronger reference, and quantify how much adherence verdicts change as a function of judge choice.

**Why it matters:** Audit methods underpin third-party verification of safety claims (a top open problem in technical AI governance). Showing whether cheap open judges suffice—or systematically distort—directly affects who can credibly run audits outside major labs.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in SpecEval (arXiv 2509.02464), which parses spec statements and uses model judges across six providers. Open-problems framing from 'Open Problems in Technical AI Governance' (third-party verifiable safety claims).

title: Replicating METR's 'Common Elements of Frontier Safety Policies' Coding Scheme on the Seoul Summit Signatories
quick_reasoning: Precisely quantifies coverage/vagueness of voluntary frontier safety commitments, a specific governance gap.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating METR's 'Common Elements of Frontier Safety Policies' Coding Scheme on the Seoul Summit Signatories

**Problem:** METR distilled common elements of frontier AI safety policies (capability thresholds, dangerous-capability evals, mitigation protocols, pause commitments). Sixteen companies committed at the Seoul Summit 2024 to publish such frameworks, but no public artifact systematically codes WHICH common elements each signatory actually included versus omitted, or how vague the commitments are.

**Direction:** Operationalize METR's common-elements list into a binary/ordinal coding scheme, then code each signatory's published safety framework against it (present / partial / absent / vague). The twist is broadening from the handful of analyzed leaders to the full Seoul cohort, plus adding a 'specificity' score per commitment. Produce a coverage matrix and a vagueness ranking.

**Why it matters:** Directly addresses the open problem of the gap between voluntary codes and enforceable standards by quantifying how hollow or substantive each lab's voluntary commitment is. Pure document analysis, no compute, high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in METR 'Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies', Seoul Summit 2024 (16 signatories), and Anthropic RSP / DeepMind FSF / Meta framework. EU Code of Practice context for the voluntary-vs-enforceable gap.

title: Replicating HELM Safety Refusal Benchmarks on Quantized Open Models to Test Whether Quantization Erodes Safety
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific deployment-safety question (does quantization erode safety/refusal) with a clean focused experiment.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating HELM Safety Refusal Benchmarks on Quantized Open Models to Test Whether Quantization Erodes Safety

**Problem:** HELM Safety standardizes LLM safety scoring across six risk categories (violence, fraud, discrimination, sexual content, harassment, deception) using XSTest, HarmBench, SimpleSafetyTest, etc. Deployers routinely run 4-bit/8-bit quantized open models on consumer hardware for cost reasons, but whether aggressive quantization degrades a model's safety/refusal behavior is rarely measured and has clear governance relevance for edge deployment.

**Direction:** Take a subset of HELM Safety scenarios and replicate them on one open model at full precision and at 4-bit/8-bit quantization. The twist is precision-as-the-variable rather than model-as-the-variable. Measure refusal-rate and over-refusal (XSTest benign) deltas across precisions, isolating whether safety alignment survives quantization.

**Why it matters:** Edge/quantized deployment is exactly where lab-level defense-in-depth is absent, so degraded safety there is a deployment-governance blind spot. Fully feasible on one consumer GPU with open tools and open models.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in HELM Safety (5 benchmarks, 6 risk categories incl. XSTest over-refusal, HarmBench jailbreaks). Quantization-vs-safety is the underexplored twist; tools are open.

title: Replicating CSET AI-Harm Incident Taxonomy Coding on a Recent Slice of the AI Incident Database
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses reliability of incident taxonomies and near-miss capture for incident-response governance.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating CSET AI-Harm Incident Taxonomy Coding on a Recent Slice of the AI Incident Database

**Problem:** The CSET AI Harm Taxonomy and the AI Incident Database support classifying incidents by sector, harm type, and lifecycle phase, and recent work uses LLMs to auto-classify with confidence ratings. But coverage and inter-rater reliability of taxonomy coding on the most RECENT incidents (generative-AI era) is under-characterized, and near-misses are inconsistently captured.

**Direction:** Take the published CSET taxonomy and replicate the coding exercise on a recent window of AIID incidents (e.g., the last 6-12 months). The twist is twofold: focus on generative-AI incidents and explicitly tag near-misses vs. realized harms. Compare your hand-coding against an LLM auto-classifier and report agreement and confidence calibration.

**Why it matters:** National AI incident-response frameworks (an explicit open problem, NTSB-for-AI analogy) depend on reliable incident taxonomies. Showing where taxonomy/near-miss coding breaks down on modern incidents is directly actionable and needs only public data.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in CSET AI Harm Taxonomy, AI Incident Database 'Scalable AI Incident Classification', GMF taxonomy (arXiv 2211.07280), and 'Designing Incident Reporting Systems for Harms from General-Purpose AI' (arXiv 2511.05914) on near-miss reporting.

title: Replicating LLM Political-Bias Measurement With the Political Compass Test on Open vs. Closed Models
quick_reasoning: Relates to AI bias/viewpoint-neutrality governance but political-bias measurement has a looser link to core catastrophic-AI-safety outcomes.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating LLM Political-Bias Measurement With the Political Compass Test on Open vs. Closed Models

**Problem:** Political-bias studies of LLMs combine standardized instruments (Political Compass Test) with repeated API querying and multi-judge evaluation, mostly on commercial models, and show widespread perceived bias. Whether OPEN-weight models—often used by self-hosters precisely to avoid vendor 'opinions'—exhibit comparable or different bias profiles, and how stable that is across prompt paraphrases, is under-tested.

**Direction:** Replicate the Political Compass / standardized-instrument methodology with repeated sampling and paraphrase perturbations, applying it to 4-5 small open-weight instruct models as the twist. Report mean stance, variance under paraphrase (prompt brittleness), and refusal-to-answer rates, and compare against published closed-model results.

**Why it matters:** Bias and viewpoint neutrality are entering regulation (e.g., government procurement rules), and self-hosted open models are a governance blind spot. Reproducible with public instruments and a single GPU, no proprietary access.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Assessing Political Bias in LLMs' (arXiv 2405.13041), 'Beyond prompt brittleness' (arXiv 2402.17649) on consistency, and OpenAI's political-bias eval framework (5 axes). Twist = open models + brittleness focus.

title: Replicating AI-Generated-Text Watermark Detection Robustness Under Simple Edits Using Open SynthID-Text
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses robustness of watermarking/provenance governance mechanisms with a focused robustness test.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating AI-Generated-Text Watermark Detection Robustness Under Simple Edits Using Open SynthID-Text

**Problem:** Provenance/watermarking is proposed as a governance mechanism, but text watermarks are known to be fragile: metadata strips and paraphrasing degrade detectability. SynthID text watermarking is now open-sourced, yet there's little accessible, reproducible evidence on exactly how much common, low-effort edits (paraphrase, translation round-trip, truncation, light insertion) erode detection for non-experts.

**Direction:** Use the open SynthID-text tooling to watermark generations from an open model, then replicate a watermark-robustness evaluation where the twist is a battery of cheap real-world transformations (paraphrase via another open model, translate-and-back, sentence shuffling, partial deletion). Plot detection AUC vs. edit strength and identify the cheapest edit that defeats detection.

**Why it matters:** Watermarking underpins provenance policy (EU AI Act labeling, content authenticity). Concrete evidence of how easily ordinary users defeat it informs whether watermark-based governance is viable. Entirely open tools, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in open-sourced SynthID text watermarking (Google DeepMind), 'On the Difficulty of Constructing a Robust and Publicly-Detectable Watermark' (arXiv 2502.04901), and C2PA provenance limitations (metadata stripping).

title: Replicating Dangerous-Capability Refusal Evals Across Model Sizes Within One Open Family to Map Scaling of Safety
quick_reasoning: Targets the capability-threshold premise that risk scales with capability via a clean within-family scaling study.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Dangerous-Capability Refusal Evals Across Model Sizes Within One Open Family to Map Scaling of Safety

**Problem:** Frontier safety frameworks (RSP/FSF) tie mitigations to capability thresholds, assuming dangerous-capability evals scale meaningfully with model capability. But the relationship between scale and refusal/dangerous-capability behavior is usually compared across heterogeneous vendors, confounding architecture and training. A clean within-family scaling study is rarely published openly.

**Direction:** Take a published dangerous-capability or refusal eval subset and replicate it across multiple sizes of a SINGLE open model family (e.g., 1B/3B/8B/70B-quantized of one release). The twist is holding training/architecture fixed and varying only scale, reporting how refusal robustness and (proxy) dangerous-capability scores change monotonically or not with size.

**Why it matters:** Capability-threshold governance assumes predictable scaling of risk; a clean within-family curve tests that premise empirically. Uses open models on a single GPU (smaller sizes + quantized large), no training.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in METR common elements / RSP / FSF capability-threshold logic and HELM Safety eval components. Within-family scaling is the methodological twist; 'Measurement challenges in AI catastrophic risk governance' (arXiv 2410.00608) motivates measurement scrutiny.

title: Replicating the MLCommons AI Safety Benchmark v0.5 on Non-English Prompts
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets cross-language consistency of safety benchmarks, key to international evaluation consensus.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the MLCommons AI Safety Benchmark v0.5 on Non-English Prompts

**Problem:** MLCommons released an AI Safety Benchmark (v0.5) with structured hazard categories and a standardized methodology, but the benchmark and most reported runs are English-centric. Whether the same hazard taxonomy yields comparable safety scores when prompts are localized to other languages—and whether ranking of models flips—is an open governance question for international evaluation consensus.

**Direction:** Replicate the MLCommons v0.5 benchmark structure on a subset of open models, with the twist of translating the prompt set into 2-3 additional languages (e.g., Spanish, Hindi, Arabic) and re-scoring. Measure per-language safety-score deltas and whether the relative ranking of models is language-invariant.

**Why it matters:** International consensus on evaluation methodology (an explicit open problem via the International Network of AI Safety Institutes) requires benchmarks that behave consistently across languages. Reproducible with open benchmark + open models on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Introducing v0.5 of the AI Safety Benchmark from MLCommons' (arXiv 2404.12241) and the International Network of AI Safety Institutes consensus goal. Twist = multilingual localization + ranking stability.

title: Replicating XSTest Over-Refusal Measurement on Heavily-Guardrailed Open Models to Quantify Safety-Tax
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses the over-refusal safety/usefulness tradeoff relevant to proportionate safety governance.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating XSTest Over-Refusal Measurement on Heavily-Guardrailed Open Models to Quantify Safety-Tax

**Problem:** XSTest measures over-refusal: models wrongly refusing benign requests that merely resemble unsafe ones. Governance debate frames a tradeoff between safety and usefulness, but the over-refusal 'safety tax' of newer, more heavily guardrailed open releases (and 'safety-tuned' community fine-tunes) versus their base instruct versions is rarely quantified head-to-head.

**Direction:** Replicate the XSTest over-refusal protocol with the twist of pairing each model with a more-guardrailed counterpart (e.g., a base instruct model vs. a community 'safety-aligned' fine-tune, or two successive versions of an open release). Report over-refusal rate deltas and characterize which benign categories trigger the most spurious refusals.

**Why it matters:** Over-refusal is the usability cost of safety mandates; quantifying it informs proportionate governance and standards that don't incentivize degraded helpfulness. Open benchmark, open models, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in XSTest (part of HELM Safety) for over-refusal measurement. Twist = paired guardrail-intensity comparison on open models to estimate a 'safety tax'.

title: Replicating Frontier-Framework Text Analysis to Track Commitment Drift Across RSP/FSF Versions Over Time
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets commitment drift/durability in safety frameworks, a specific governance concern.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Frontier-Framework Text Analysis to Track Commitment Drift Across RSP/FSF Versions Over Time

**Problem:** Labs revise their safety frameworks (e.g., Anthropic RSP v1 to v3, DeepMind FSF 1.0 to 2.0). Analyses typically assess the LATEST version, but whether commitments strengthen, soften, or get hedged across versions—'commitment drift'—is not systematically tracked, despite being central to whether voluntary commitments are durable.

**Direction:** Replicate a structured framework-coding analysis (capability thresholds, pause commitments, eval triggers, escape hatches) but apply it longitudinally across consecutive versions of 2-3 labs' frameworks. The twist is the time dimension: diff successive versions, classify each change as strengthening/softening/clarifying, and quantify net drift per lab.

**Why it matters:** Durability of voluntary commitments is the crux of the voluntary-vs-enforceable gap (an explicit open problem). Showing systematic softening would be a strong governance signal. Pure document analysis, no compute, high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in Anthropic RSP v3.0 analysis (GovAI), DeepMind FSF 2.0, METR common elements, and the EU Code of Practice voluntary-vs-enforceable framing. Twist = longitudinal version diffing.

title: Replicating an LLM-as-Auditor Pipeline for Incident Classification With a Calibration Twist
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses calibration of automated incident classifiers underpinning incident-response systems.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating an LLM-as-Auditor Pipeline for Incident Classification With a Calibration Twist

**Problem:** Recent AIID work uses LLMs to classify incidents against risk taxonomies and emits a confidence rating, but whether those confidence ratings are CALIBRATED (i.e., 70%-confidence classifications are right ~70% of the time) is rarely checked. Miscalibrated automated classifiers could silently corrupt the evidence base national incident-response systems would rely on.

**Direction:** Replicate an LLM-based incident-classification pipeline on a labeled subset of AIID incidents using an open model, then add the twist of a calibration analysis: bin predictions by self-reported confidence and plot reliability curves, comparing the open model against a stronger reference. Report Brier score and over/under-confidence by taxonomy category.

**Why it matters:** Trustworthy automated triage is a prerequisite for scalable incident reporting (NTSB-for-AI open problem). Calibration is exactly the kind of unglamorous but decision-critical evaluation labs deprioritize. Open data, open model, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Scalable AI Incident Classification' (incidentdatabase.ai, LLM classification with confidence ratings) and CSET AI Harm Taxonomy. Twist = calibration/reliability analysis of the auto-classifier.

title: Replicating Multilingual Political-Stance Steering Findings on Small Open Models Using Activation-Free Prompting
quick_reasoning: Relates to neutrality/manipulation governance but cross-lingual political-stance steering has an indirect link to core safety outcomes.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Multilingual Political-Stance Steering Findings on Small Open Models Using Activation-Free Prompting

**Problem:** Work on multilingual political views shows LLM ideology can shift across languages and be steered, but steering studies often use activation-level interventions requiring engineering depth. For governance, the more deployment-relevant question is whether ordinary prompt-level framing in different languages shifts a model's expressed policy stances—accessible to any user and any regulator-style auditor.

**Direction:** Replicate the cross-lingual political-stance finding using only PROMPT-level manipulations (no activation steering) on 3-4 small open models. The twist is restricting interventions to user-accessible prompting in 3 languages and measuring stance shift on a fixed policy-statement battery, isolating the language effect from the intervention-sophistication effect.

**Why it matters:** If trivial multilingual prompting shifts policy stances, neutrality regulation premised on a single-language audit is inadequate. Uses only open models and prompting, no interpretability expertise, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Multilingual Political Views of LLMs: Identification and Steering' (arXiv 2507.22623) and 'Bias Beyond Borders' (arXiv 2601.23001). Twist = prompt-only, beginner-accessible replication.

title: Replicating Safety-Leaderboard Gaming on a Small Scale to Demonstrate Benchmark Fragility for Auditors
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets gameability of safety benchmarks undermining third-party verification.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Safety-Leaderboard Gaming on a Small Scale to Demonstrate Benchmark Fragility for Auditors

**Problem:** Research warns that fully-open safety benchmarks (like HELM) can be gamed: even small models fine-tuned on the public eval data can top specific scenarios. Governance increasingly cites leaderboard scores, yet there's little accessible, reproducible demonstration of how easily a determined developer could inflate a safety score without genuinely improving safety.

**Direction:** Replicate the leaderboard-gaming finding at small scale: take a public safety-eval subset, lightly tune or prompt-engineer a small open model specifically against that subset, then evaluate on a held-out disjoint safety set. The twist is contrasting in-distribution (gamed) vs. out-of-distribution safety scores to expose the inflation, framed as an auditor's red-flag checklist.

**Why it matters:** Third-party verification of safety claims (a top open problem) is undermined if scores are gameable. A clear, reproducible demonstration plus auditor guidance is directly useful and needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Pitfalls of Evaluating Language Models with Open Benchmarks' (arXiv 2507.00460) and HELM gaming concerns (small cheating models topping scenarios). Twist = small-scale reproducible demo + auditor checklist.

title: Replicating Dangerous-Knowledge Refusal Evals With a System-Prompt-Only Mitigation to Test the 'Prompts Aren't Controls' Claim
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific load-bearing governance assumption about where safety controls must live with a clean test.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Dangerous-Knowledge Refusal Evals With a System-Prompt-Only Mitigation to Test the 'Prompts Aren't Controls' Claim

**Problem:** EU AI Act compliance discussions assert that system-prompt instructions are 'natural-language suggestions, not security controls' and that restrictions must be enforced at the API level. This is widely repeated but rarely demonstrated with a clean, reproducible head-to-head on open models showing how much (or little) a system-prompt-only safety policy actually holds under mild adversarial pressure.

**Direction:** Replicate a refusal/jailbreak eval on an open model under two conditions: (a) safety relying only on a system-prompt policy, and (b) the model's built-in alignment. The twist is treating the system-prompt-as-control claim as the hypothesis under test, measuring how quickly simple jailbreak templates erode each condition's refusal rate.

**Why it matters:** Directly stress-tests a load-bearing governance assumption about where safety controls must live, informing deployment-practice standards. Uses open models and public jailbreak prompts on a single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in EU AI Act compliance analyses stating system prompts are not security controls, and STACK 'Adversarial Attacks on LLM Safeguard Pipelines' (arXiv 2506.24068). Twist = empirical test of the prompt-as-control claim on open models.

title: Replicating Refusal-Category Coverage From Model Specs as a Behavioral Eval on Open Models
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses whether open models meet the refusal-category structure regulators expect.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Refusal-Category Coverage From Model Specs as a Behavioral Eval on Open Models

**Problem:** The EU GPAI Code of Practice expects model specifications to enumerate refusal categories and a principle hierarchy, and OpenAI/Anthropic publish such categories. But open-weight models usually have no spec, so it's unknown how well their actual refusal behavior maps onto the standardized refusal-category taxonomy that regulators are converging on.

**Direction:** Take a published refusal-category taxonomy (from a frontier model spec / Code of Practice), turn each category into a small probe set, and replicate it as a behavioral eval on 3-4 open models. The twist is using a spec-derived taxonomy as the measurement frame for spec-less models, producing a category-by-model refusal-coverage heatmap.

**Why it matters:** Maps whether open models implicitly satisfy the refusal-category structure regulators expect, informing whether spec-style requirements are realistic for the open ecosystem. Open taxonomy, open models, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in EU GPAI Code of Practice (model spec must include refusal categories, principle hierarchy, system prompts) and published frontier model specs. Twist = applying a spec-derived refusal taxonomy to spec-less open models.

title: Replicating the AI Safety Index's 'Information Sharing' Domain as a Citation/Disclosure Audit Across Labs Over Two Editions
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses reproducible disclosure metrics for third-party safety verification.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the AI Safety Index's 'Information Sharing' Domain as a Citation/Disclosure Audit Across Labs Over Two Editions

**Problem:** The AI Safety Index scores an 'Information Sharing' domain (technical disclosures, policy engagement) but the underlying disclosure evidence is summarized by experts, not exposed as a reproducible audit trail. There's no public, replicable dataset of what each lab actually disclosed (system cards, eval results, policy submissions) and how that changed between Index editions.

**Direction:** Replicate the Information Sharing scoring as a transparent disclosure audit: for 5-6 labs, enumerate and tally public disclosures (system/model cards, eval reports, policy comment submissions) across two time points. The twist is constructing a reproducible disclosure tally and comparing it against the Index's expert grade to check whether grades track countable disclosure behavior.

**Why it matters:** Reproducible disclosure metrics support third-party verification and reduce reliance on opaque expert judgment, advancing auditable safety-claim verification (a top open problem). Pure public-document work, no compute.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in FLI AI Safety Index Information Sharing domain across Summer/Winter 2025 editions. Twist = building a reproducible, countable disclosure-tally audit and validating it against expert grades.

title: Replicating Multilingual Safety-Transfer Analysis With Code-Switching as the Twist
quick_reasoning: Targets a realistic multilingual guardrail-evasion threat (code-switching) with a focused refusal-rate experiment.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Multilingual Safety-Transfer Analysis With Code-Switching as the Twist

**Problem:** Multilingual safety work attributes weak non-English guardrails to English-centric RLHF data. Most studies test clean single-language prompts, but real users in bilingual regions code-switch (mix languages within a sentence). Whether code-switching—rather than full translation—uniquely degrades safety is a realistic, under-tested governance concern.

**Direction:** Replicate the multilingual refusal-rate methodology but with the twist of code-switched prompts (e.g., Spanish-English, Hindi-English intra-sentence mixing) versus monolingual baselines on open models. Measure whether code-switching produces refusal-rate degradation beyond what either language alone causes, and characterize which mixing patterns are most evasive.

**Why it matters:** Captures a realistic multilingual-deployment threat that mono-lingual evaluations (and most lab safety pipelines) miss, supporting international evaluation standards. Open models + translation, single GPU, no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Multilingual Jailbreak Challenges' (ICLR24) and 'Towards Safe Multilingual Frontier AI' (arXiv 2409.13708). Twist = code-switching rather than full-language translation.
